meaning: Doing something while relying on someone or something as your support or clue: “relying on ...”, “guided by ...”.

senses.label: Guided by a clue
senses.meaning: Using a map, a light, a memory, etc. as a clue or means to do something. Often used when feeling your way through a difficult or unclear situation. Slightly literary; common in narration.
senses.connection: Noun + を頼りに／を頼りにして (common: 地図・明かり・記憶・勘・手がかり)
examples: Relying on the map, I finally made it to the hotel.
By the light of a flashlight, I walked along the dark mountain path.
Relying on my faint memories, I looked for the house I used to live in.

senses.label: Relying on a person
senses.meaning: Treating someone as the person you depend on. As a predicate, 「〜を頼りにする」 means “to count on someone”. It carries trust and expectation.
senses.connection: Person + を頼りに(する／している)
examples: He moved to Tokyo, counting on his uncle for help.
Everyone on the team is counting on you.

notes: 「頼り」 itself is a noun. 「頼りになる」 means “reliable”. It has no 「を」, so it is not this pattern.
「を頼りに」 is followed by an action verb (探す・歩く・進む, etc.). 「を頼りにする」 means “to depend on someone”.
「〜を頼りとして」 is also possible and sounds more formal.

daily.title: Finding your way on a trip
daily.description: Using a phone map in an unfamiliar city.
daily.example: Using the map on my phone, I walked to the station.

daily.title: Telling a friend you trust them
daily.description: Said when asking a reliable friend for help.
daily.example: Whenever I'm in trouble, I always count on you.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: Describing a character feeling their way in the dark.
daily.example: Guided by the starlight, she made her way through the forest.

work.title: Investigation report
work.description: Explaining an investigation based on limited clues.
work.example: Working from a few small clues, we pressed on with finding the cause.

work.title: Talking to a new project lead
work.description: A boss expressing expectations of a team member.
work.example: We're counting on you for the new project, you know.

etymology: 「頼り」 is the noun form (masu-stem) of the verb 「頼る」 (to rely on), meaning “something to rely on”. With 「を〜に」, it became a set phrase: “taking ... as your support”.

similar.title: 〜をもとに(して)
similar.explanation: 「〜をもとに」 means using something as material or a basis to create something (小説・資料). 「〜を頼りに」 means relying on it as a clue in order to act in a difficult situation.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「〜に基づいて」 means based on rules or facts; it is objective and formal. 「〜を頼りに」 has a subjective feeling of “this is all I have to go on”.

similar.title: 〜を通して
similar.explanation: 「〜を通して」 means through some medium or means. 「〜を頼りに」 stresses depending on it as a support or clue.

title: 〜ままに (going along with / just as)
meaning: Acting as your will, feelings, or someone's instructions lead you, or doing something exactly as it is: “as ... pleases”, “just as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form, Noun + の + ままに

senses.label: Going along with
senses.meaning: Acting on your feelings, desires, or someone's orders without holding back. It often suggests “doing whatever you like” or “being pushed around”. Mostly written or narrative.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ままに (気の向く・足の向く・思う・言われる) / Noun + の + ままに (心の・欲望の)
examples: I set off alone on a trip, wherever my mood took me.
I did whatever the clerk said and ended up signing up for an expensive plan.
He lives by his desires.

senses.label: Just as it was
senses.meaning: Doing something exactly as you saw or felt it, without embellishing: “honestly, as it is”. Often with 「見た」「感じた」「思った」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ままに (見た・感じた・思った・聞いた)
examples: Please tell us exactly what you saw.
If you write just what you felt, it will make a good essay.

notes: 「〜たままにする／ておく」 means “leave as is” (窓を開けたままにする). That is the basic use of 「まま」, not this pattern.
「に」 can be dropped: 「言われるまま、」「思うまま」.
「〜られるままに」 means passively letting others push you around. It sounds more negative.

daily.title: Talking about travel plans
daily.description: Answering a friend who asks where you're going.
daily.example: I don't have any plans. I'll just walk wherever my feet take me.

daily.title: Regretting an impulse buy
daily.description: Complaining to family about a pushy salesperson.
daily.example: I just went along with what the clerk recommended and bought three outfits.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: Describing a character following their heart.
daily.example: As his heart commanded, the boy started running toward the sea.

work.title: Accident investigation
work.description: Asking a witness for an honest account.
work.example: Please just tell us exactly what you saw.

work.title: Criticizing a team member
work.description: Pointing out a lack of backbone.
work.example: If you give discounts whenever customers ask, we won't make a profit.

etymology: 「まま」 is written 「儘」 and originally meant “as it is; as one wishes”. Old Japanese 「心のまま」 meant “as the heart wishes”. Adding 「に」 makes it adverbial: “going along with ...”.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: The basic meaning of 「〜まま」 is “keeping a state unchanged” (靴を履いたまま入る). 「〜ままに」 focuses on acting according to a will, or exactly as something is.

similar.title: 〜とおりに
similar.explanation: 「〜とおりに」 is a neutral “just as ...”. 「〜ままに」 often adds a sense of “uncontrolled, going along with” or “unembellished”.

similar.title: 〜られるままに
similar.explanation: 「〜られるままに」 stresses passively letting others control you. It is a more negative version of the “going along with” meaning.

meaning: Something has enough value to deserve an action: “worthy of ...”, “deserves ...”. Mostly written.
connection: Noun / Verb dictionary form + に値する

senses.label: Worthy of (noun)
senses.meaning: Means “has the value of ...”. Usually follows a Sino-Japanese noun of evaluation or action. Formal; common in reviews and the news.
senses.connection: Noun + に値する (称賛・注目・尊敬・一読・検討)
examples: His brave action deserves praise.
This book is worth reading.
I think that proposal is well worth considering.

senses.label: Worthy of (verb)
senses.meaning: Attaches directly to a verb: “worth doing”. Often with 「信頼する」「尊敬する」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に値する
examples: He is a person worthy of trust.
This movie is worth watching no matter how many times you see it.

senses.label: Not worth
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜に値しない」 means “not worth ...”. It is a clearly negative judgment.
senses.connection: Noun / Verb dictionary form + に値しない
examples: Such rumors aren't worth discussing.
His excuses aren't worth listening to.

notes: 「値」 is read 「あたい」 here, not 「ね」. In 「値段」 and 「値上げ」, 「値（ね）」 means “price”.
Mostly used for positive or formal evaluations. In everyday speech, people usually say 「〜する価値がある」.
Before a noun: 「信頼に値する人」「注目に値する点」.

daily.title: Recommending a book
daily.description: Recommending a good book to a friend.
daily.example: This novel is worth reading. You should definitely try it.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A commentator evaluating someone's actions.
daily.example: The boy's brave action deserves praise.

work.title: Evaluating a proposal in a meeting
work.description: Supporting a colleague's plan.
work.example: I think this plan is worth considering.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Pointing out noteworthy data.
work.example: This result is worthy of attention.

etymology: 「値（あたい）」 originally means “value, price”. 「〜に値する」 literally means “to have value equal to ...”, hence “to deserve”.

similar.title: 〜に足る
similar.explanation: 「〜に足る」 means “enough to ...; qualified for ...” (信頼に足る). It is more literary and stresses being good enough. 「〜に値する」 stresses having value.

similar.title: 〜がい（甲斐）
similar.explanation: 「〜がい」 is the meaning or reward you feel from doing something (やりがい); it is subjective. 「〜に値する」 is an objective judgment of worth.

similar.title: 〜価値がある
similar.explanation: 「〜する価値がある」 is the common spoken phrase with a similar meaning. 「〜に値する」 is more formal and concise.

meaning: “If it were ..., that would be one thing (understandable), but this case is not OK.” Contrasts two situations.
connection: Noun / plain form + ならともかく

senses.label: Contrasting people
senses.meaning: The first part is someone or something understandable or forgivable; the second is unacceptable. The second clause usually expresses dissatisfaction or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun + ならともかく、〜 (子ども・素人・初心者, etc.)
examples: It'd be one thing for a child, but for an adult to do something like that...
An amateur might be excused, but a professional shouldn't make a mistake like this.

senses.label: Contrasting situations
senses.meaning: The first part is a hypothetical or past situation (“that would be fine”); the second points out that reality is different.
senses.connection: Noun / Verb / Adjective plain form + ならともかく
examples: That might have worked in the old days, but that approach won't work now.
Once would be one thing, but being late every day is a problem.
If you were busy, fine, but not helping when you're free just isn't right.

notes: The second clause is usually negative, critical, or about something hard to accept.
「〜はともかく」 means “setting ... aside” and puts a topic aside. 「〜ならともかく」 focuses on the contrast “if it were ..., it'd be OK”.
「〜ならとにかく」 is also used, with the same meaning.

daily.title: Criticizing a friend
daily.description: A friend acting immaturely.
daily.example: A student might get away with it, but that attitude isn't OK for a working adult.

daily.title: Talking about getting somewhere
daily.description: Hesitating about going far.
daily.example: If it were close by, sure, but walking all that way is impossible.

work.title: Pointing out a basic mistake
work.description: A boss criticizing a veteran employee.
work.example: From a new hire, fine, but I can't believe a veteran like you made this mistake.

work.title: Discussing deadlines
work.description: Explaining that a deadline is too tight.
work.example: A week might work, but finishing it in three days is tough.

etymology: 「ともかく」 is written 「兎も角」 and originally meant “anyway; setting aside”. With the conditional 「なら」, it means “if it were ..., we could set it aside”, which creates the contrast.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: 「〜はともかく」 means “... aside”, setting one topic aside to talk about another. 「〜ならともかく」 means “if it were ..., it'd be acceptable”, in contrast with reality.

similar.title: 〜ならまだしも
similar.explanation: 「〜ならまだしも」 is very close (“would still be better”), but stronger and more formal (N1).

similar.title: 〜ならいざしらず
similar.explanation: 「〜ならいざしらず」 is more literary, often used as “special cases aside, normally ...”.

title: 〜ざる (+ noun)
meaning: The noun-modifying form of the classical negative 「ず」. It modifies a noun: “that does not ...; un-...”. Used in writing, literature, and set phrases.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ざる + Noun (する→せざる)

senses.label: That does not ...
senses.meaning: Equivalent to modern 「〜ない + noun」. Solemn and literary; common in titles, ads, and the news.
senses.connection: Verb nai-stem + ざる + Noun (知られざる・見えざる・招かれざる・絶えざる)
examples: This program uncovers the hidden truths of history.
He was an uninvited guest.
An invisible hand is at work in the market.

senses.label: Set phrases
senses.meaning: Used in some fixed expressions and proverbs. 「せざる」 is the form for 「する」.
senses.connection: せざる + Noun (予期せざる・意図せざる) / set phrases (働かざる者食うべからず)
examples: An unexpected situation occurred.
He who does not work shall not eat.
Behind his success lay his unceasing effort.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せざる」, never 「しざる」.
「〜ざるを得ない」 (“have no choice but to”) is a different pattern. Don't mix them up.
The 「ざる」 in 「ざるそば」 and 「ざるに上げる」 means “bamboo strainer” and has nothing to do with negation.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: A program title uses classical language.
daily.example: I watched a program called “Japan's Unknown Great Castles”.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: Describing an unwelcome visitor.
daily.example: That night, an uninvited guest appeared at the mansion.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting a sudden incident.
work.example: Service was suspended due to unexpected trouble.

work.title: Giving a speech
work.description: Recognizing employees' hard work.
work.example: Thank you all for your unceasing efforts.

etymology: The classical negative 「ず」 had an extra set of forms (ざら・ざり・ざる・ざれ), which came from 「ず + あり」. 「ざる」 is its noun-modifying form. In modern Japanese it survives only in writing and set phrases.

similar.title: 〜ぬ (negative)
similar.explanation: 「ぬ」 is also a classical negative and can modify nouns (知らぬ人). It is a bit lighter and more common; 「ざる」 is more solemn and literary.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Followed by 「を得ない」, 「ざる」 forms the set pattern “have no choice but to”. In this entry, 「ざる」 directly modifies a noun.

similar.title: 〜べからず／〜べからざる
similar.explanation: 「べからざる」 is the negative noun-modifying form of 「べし」: “that must not ...” (欠くべからざる = indispensable). It is a separate pattern.

meaning: Doing something else on the way to or from somewhere, or just as you're leaving: “on the way ...”, “just as ... leaving”.
connection: Masu-stem of certain verbs + がけに (帰り・行き・通り・出)

senses.label: On the way
senses.meaning: Doing something on the way there or back. Only used with a few movement verbs like 「帰る」「行く」「通る」. Used in both speech and writing.
senses.connection: 帰りがけに／行きがけに／通りがけに
examples: On my way home from work, I did some shopping at the supermarket.
On my way to the station, I mailed a letter.
As I passed by, I took a quick look inside the shop.

senses.label: Just as you leave
senses.meaning: 「出がけに」 means “just as you are going out”. Often followed by something unexpected, or by something done quickly before leaving.
senses.connection: 出がけに (＝出かけるときに)
examples: Just as I was leaving, I got a phone call and ended up being late.
As I was going out, my mom told me to take an umbrella.

notes: Only a few verbs work, mainly 「帰り・行き・通り・出」. You can't freely say 「✕食べがけに」.
It can also be a noun: 「帰りがけの駄賃」「出がけの電話」.
「〜かけ(る)」 means “half-done” (読みかけの本). That is a different pattern.

daily.title: Asking family to pick something up
daily.description: A call to a family member before they come home.
daily.example: Can you pick up some milk on your way home?

daily.title: Dropping in
daily.description: Passing near a friend's house.
daily.example: I was passing by, so I thought I'd drop in. How are you?

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend.
daily.example: It started raining just as I was leaving, so I was changing clothes.

work.title: An errand on the way
work.description: Telling a coworker you'll stop at the post office after work.
work.example: I'll stop by the post office on my way home and send the documents.

work.title: On the way to work
work.description: Reporting a client visit on the way in.
work.example: On my way to the office this morning, I dropped off some materials at a client's.

etymology: 「がけ」 is the voiced form of 「掛け（かけ）」. 「掛け」 can mean “at the time of ...”. Combined with 「帰り」「行き」, etc., it forms 「帰りがけ」: “when going home; on the way back”.

similar.title: 〜ついでに
similar.explanation: 「〜ついでに」 means using the chance of doing A to also do B, and works in many situations (買い物のついでに). 「〜がけに」 is limited to the way there or back, or when leaving.

similar.title: 〜途中で
similar.explanation: 「〜途中で」 just objectively means “on the way”. 「〜がけに」 often implies “while you're at it”.

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: 「〜がてら」 means doing B along with A, where A is also a goal (散歩がてら). 「〜がけに」 points to a moment during a trip.

title: 〜ては・〜ていては (if ..., bad result)
meaning: “If (you keep) doing this, something bad will happen.” The second clause is usually negative.
connection: Verb te-form / い-adj くて / Noun で + は; Verb te-form + いては

senses.label: If ..., it'll be bad
senses.meaning: Sets up a condition and points out a bad result. The second clause is often 「困る」「だめだ」「〜ない」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は (casual: 〜ちゃ／〜じゃ)
examples: If you eat that much, you'll gain weight.
If you quit now, all your effort so far will go to waste.

senses.label: If you keep this up
senses.meaning: 「〜ていては」 stresses that if a state continues, you won't get a good result. Often a warning or criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いては
examples: If you play around every day, you won't pass.
If all you do is complain, nothing will change.

senses.label: With things like this
senses.meaning: Attaches to adjectives and nouns: “if the situation is like this, (it won't work)”.
senses.connection: い-adj くて + は / Noun・な-adj で + は
examples: When it's this hot, it's impossible to get any work done.
With these grades, passing will be hard.

notes: The second clause must be a bad result. It can't be positive (✕練習しては上手になる).
In casual speech, 「ては」 becomes 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 becomes 「じゃ」: 「そんなに食べちゃ太るよ」.
「〜ては〜」 also has a “repeated action” use (書いては消す). That is different.

daily.title: Telling family to go to bed
daily.description: A parent talking to a child who stays up late.
daily.example: If you keep staying up that late, you'll ruin your health.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about the rain.
daily.example: With rain going on like this, the laundry won't dry.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend wants to give up studying.
daily.example: It'd be such a waste to give up now.

work.title: Advice from a boss
work.description: Pointing out a problem with how someone works.
work.example: If you keep handling everything alone, the work will never get done.

work.title: Discussing the budget
work.description: Explaining that the budget isn't enough.
work.example: With this budget, it will be hard to carry out the plan.

etymology: 「ては」 is the particle 「て」 plus the topic particle 「は」. 「は」 singles out the condition, stressing “once this is the case”, so it often leads to a bad result.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜では (bad result)
similar.explanation: The N3 entry for the same use. This entry adds 「〜ていては」 for continuing states.

similar.title: 〜ていては
similar.explanation: An entry just for 「〜ていては」, stressing “if this keeps going”. This entry also covers 「〜ては」 and 「〜では」.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「〜たら」 is a neutral conditional; the result can be good or bad. 「〜ては」 is only followed by bad results.

similar.title: 〜ては (repetition)
similar.explanation: 「書いては消す」 shows an action repeated over and over. It has nothing to do with conditions.

meaning: The degree goes beyond a standard (an expectation or something being compared): “more than ...”, “beyond ...”.
connection: Noun / Verb plain form + 以上に（の）

senses.label: More than expected
senses.meaning: Reality goes beyond what was expected or hoped for. Often with 「予想」「想像」「期待」「思った」. Before a noun, use 「以上の」.
senses.connection: 予想以上に／想像以上に／思った以上に／期待以上の + Noun
examples: The exam was harder than I expected.
He was even more capable than I had thought.
The results exceeded expectations.

senses.label: Even more than
senses.meaning: Uses the first part as a benchmark and says the second is greater. Common in phrases like “more important than ...” or “work harder than last year”.
senses.connection: Noun + 以上に (それ以上に・去年以上に・仕事以上に)
examples: This year, I want to work even harder than last year.
Money matters, but health matters even more.

notes: After a number, 「以上」 means “or more” (20歳以上). That is a range, not this pattern.
「〜以上(は)」 means “now that ...; since ...” (約束した以上は守る). That is also a different pattern.
「以上に」 is followed by a predicate; 「以上の」 is followed by a noun.

daily.title: Talking about a trip
daily.description: Sharing your impressions with a friend.
daily.example: Kyoto was an even more beautiful city than I'd imagined.

daily.title: Caring for family
daily.description: Asking your parents to look after themselves.
daily.example: Take care of your health, even more than your work, OK?

work.title: Reporting results
work.description: Reporting sales to your boss.
work.example: Sales this month grew more than expected.

work.title: New Year's speech
work.description: The president encouraging employees.
work.example: This year, let's aim for even better results than last year.

etymology: 「以上」 originally means “above this”. As a standard of comparison, 「〜以上に」 means “even more than ...”: the degree goes past it.

similar.title: 〜以上に (going beyond)
similar.explanation: Another entry for the same pattern, with the same focus: going beyond a standard.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: 「〜以上は」 means “since ..., then ...”, a cause-and-effect relation. 「〜以上に」 compares degree.

similar.title: 〜にもまして
similar.explanation: 「〜にもまして」 means “even more than ...”, often in 「何にもまして」「以前にもまして」. More formal (N1).

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: 「〜より」 is a general comparison. 「〜以上に」 stresses going beyond an expectation or standard.

meaning: The conditional 「ば」 plus 「と思う」 means “it would be nice if ...”. Often used to express wishes or requests politely and indirectly.
connection: Verb ba-form + と思う／と存じます

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜ていただければと思います」 doesn't say “please ...” directly; it says “it would be great if you could ...”. Extremely common in business emails; polite and soft.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただければと思います／存じます
examples: I would appreciate it if you could check this.
We would be grateful if you could consider it.
I'd appreciate it if you could get in touch when you have time.

senses.label: Your own wish
senses.meaning: The speaker humbly states a hope: “I hope I can ...”. Often with 「お役に立てれば」「力になれれば」.
senses.connection: Potential verb ba-form + と思う (なれれば・立てれば・できれば)
examples: I hope I can be of some help.
I hope I can put this experience to use in my work.

senses.label: Motive
senses.meaning: 「〜ばと思って／思い」 means “hoping that ...”, explaining why you did something.
senses.connection: 〜ばと思って／〜ばと思い、〜
examples: I sent the materials, hoping they might be useful.
Hoping it would make them happy, I made a homemade cake.

notes: Much softer than 「〜てください」. A standard phrase in business emails.
「〜たらと思います」 is also used (ご検討いただけたらと思います); slightly more conversational.
「〜ば幸いです」 is similar, but more formal and even more polite.

daily.title: Giving a present
daily.description: Explaining your thoughts to a friend.
daily.example: I picked it hoping you'd like it.

daily.title: Asking a friend for a favor
daily.description: Asking a friend to look at something when they're free.
daily.example: I was hoping you could take a look when you have time.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Asking a client to check an attachment.
work.example: I would appreciate it if you could review the attached materials.

work.title: Self-introduction
work.description: A new employee stating their resolve.
work.example: I hope to be of help to all of you as soon as possible.

work.title: Meeting invitation
work.description: Inviting someone to attend.
work.example: We would be delighted if you could attend.

etymology: It's the conditional 「〜ば」 plus quoting 「と思う」: “I think if ... (it would be good)”. The result, such as 「いい」 or 「幸いだ」, is left out, which makes it an indirect wish or request.

similar.title: 〜ていただけるとありがたい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ありがたい」 clearly says “I'd be grateful”. 「〜ばと思います」 leaves the result unsaid, so it's more indirect.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただけませんか」 is a direct request in question form. 「〜ばと思います」 states your wish, so it's softer.

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: 「〜ばいい」 is advice: “you just need to ...”. 「〜ばと思う」 expresses a wish or a polite request.

meaning: An affectionate, casual version of 「〜てください」: “please ... (for me)”. Mostly used with family, children, or close friends.
connection: Verb te-form + ちょうだい; Noun + をちょうだい

senses.label: Please do ... for me
senses.meaning: An affectionate request. Often used by women, or by adults to children; it sounds gentle. Never use it with superiors or customers.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ちょうだい
examples: Give me a hand for a second.
Get up already. You'll be late.

senses.label: Don't ...
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜ないでちょうだい」 is a gentle way to say “please don't ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でちょうだい
examples: Please don't say things like that.
It's dangerous, so don't play there.

senses.label: Give me something
senses.meaning: 「Noun + をちょうだい」 means “give me ...”, an affectionate form of 「〜をください」. Common when children ask their parents for things.
senses.connection: Noun + を(も)ちょうだい
examples: Mom, can I have a snack?
Give me one too.

notes: Mainly used by women, older people, and children. Men usually say 「〜てくれ」 or 「〜て」 instead.
As a humble verb, 「頂戴する」 means “to receive” (お名刺を頂戴します). That is different from this pattern.
The kanji is 「頂戴」, but in spoken requests it is usually written in kana.

daily.title: Mother to child
daily.description: Telling a child to tidy up.
daily.example: Put your toys away, please.

daily.title: Child to parent
daily.description: Wanting something to drink.
daily.example: Mommy, can I have that juice?

daily.title: Wife to husband
daily.description: A reminder before he goes out.
daily.example: Pick up some eggs on your way home, OK?

work.title: Seen in a TV drama
work.description: A female boss talking to a team member she's close to.
work.example: Put this document together by tomorrow, would you?

etymology: 「頂戴」 originally meant raising something above your head to receive it respectfully, and became a humble word for “receive”. Later 「〜てちょうだい」 was used for requests (“let me receive your ...”) and gradually turned into an affectionate, casual request.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 「〜てください」 is the standard polite request for most situations. 「〜てちょうだい」 is only for people close to you; casual and affectionate.

similar.title: 〜てくれ
similar.explanation: 「〜てくれ」 is a request in command form, common among men, and sounds blunt. 「〜てちょうだい」 is softer and tends to be used by women or older people.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: 「〜なさい」 is a command from above (早く寝なさい). 「〜てちょうだい」 is a request and sounds softer.

meaning: Someone or something tends to show a certain quality, or things overall are moving in a certain direction: “tend to ...”, “there is a trend toward ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form, Noun + の + 傾向がある; Noun + 傾向にある

senses.label: Tend to
senses.meaning: Someone or something easily shows a certain quality or behavior. Usually an objective description; it can describe negative things too.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + 傾向がある; Noun + の + 傾向がある
examples: Young people these days tend not to read newspapers.
He tends to see things pessimistically.

senses.label: Be on a trend
senses.meaning: 「〜傾向にある」 means things overall are in a trend of change. Often with Sino-Japanese nouns like 「増加」「減少」「上昇」. Common in statistics and the news.
senses.connection: Noun + 傾向にある (増加・減少・上昇・低下)
examples: Japan's population is on a downward trend.
The number of tourists from overseas is on the rise.

senses.label: A clear tendency
senses.meaning: 「傾向が強い」 and 「傾向が見られる」 describe how strong a tendency is, or that one is observed. Common in reports.
senses.connection: 〜傾向が強い／〜傾向が見られる
examples: The more urban the area, the stronger the trend toward marrying late.
An aging trend can be seen in this region.

notes: 「傾向がある」 usually describes qualities and habits; 「傾向にある」 usually describes trends in data.
Objective and rather formal. When talking about people in speech, 「〜がち」 or 「〜やすい」 is common.
For bad habits, written Japanese also has 「〜きらいがある」, which sounds critical.

daily.title: Talking about yourself
daily.description: Telling a friend about a bad habit.
daily.example: I tend to put everything off.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A report on price changes.
daily.example: They say vegetable prices are on the rise.

work.title: Market analysis report
work.description: Describing consumer behavior.
work.example: Younger generations show a strong tendency to compare products online.

work.title: Reporting in a meeting
work.description: Reporting changes in the data.
work.example: The number of inquiries has been on the rise over the past few years.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Describing research results.
work.example: The older the person, the shorter their sleep tended to be.

etymology: 「傾向」 is a Sino-Japanese word. It originally means “the direction of a slope” and came to mean “the direction things develop” or “a leaning in character”.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: 「〜がち」 usually describes bad things that happen often, and is more casual (忘れがち). 「〜傾向がある」 is objective and neutral, and works for statistics.

similar.title: 〜きらいがある
similar.explanation: 「〜きらいがある」 is only for bad tendencies and sounds critical. Very formal (N1).

similar.title: 〜気味
similar.explanation: 「〜気味」 means “a bit ...; a touch of ...” (風邪気味), describing a current state. 「〜傾向」 describes long-term qualities or trends.

similar.title: 〜やすい
similar.explanation: 「〜やすい」 means “easy to ...”, focusing on ease. 「〜傾向がある」 focuses on a tendency that often shows up.

meaning: Attached to a verb's masu-stem, it means the value, meaning, or reward of doing something: “worth doing”, “rewarding to ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + がい (がある／がない)

senses.label: Worth doing
senses.meaning: Doing something pays off or feels meaningful. Usually 「〜がいがある」; the negative is 「〜がいがない」. It carries a personal sense of satisfaction.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + がいがある (教えがい・作りがい・待ちがい・頑張りがい)
examples: The students are so eager that teaching them is really rewarding.
Everyone eats with such enjoyment that cooking for them is worth it.
No matter how hard I try, nobody recognizes it. There's no point in trying like this.

senses.label: Set nouns
senses.meaning: Some have become fixed nouns for meaning and motivation in life and work. The most common are 「生きがい」「やりがい」「働きがい」.
senses.connection: 生きがい／やりがい／働きがい + がある・を感じる・のある〜
examples: Watching her grandchild grow up is what my grandmother lives for.
I'm looking for a rewarding job.

notes: The kanji is 「甲斐」, but after verbs it is usually written in kana.
On its own it is read 「かい」: 「努力した甲斐があった」 (the effort paid off). See 「〜かいがある」.
Mainly used with volitional verbs. You can't say 「✕降りがい」.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Telling a friend that growing vegetables is fun.
daily.example: When the vegetables I water every day grow, it's really rewarding.

daily.title: Talking about life
daily.description: An older person talking about retirement.
daily.example: Calligraphy, my hobby, is what I live for now.

work.title: Job interview
work.description: Explaining why you're changing jobs.
work.example: I'd like to take on more rewarding work.

work.title: HR survey
work.description: A company paying attention to how employees feel.
work.example: We are building a workplace where employees can find their work rewarding.

etymology: 「甲斐（かい）」 originally means “effect, reward”. It is thought to be related to the verb 「替ふ」 (to exchange): “what you get in exchange for your effort”. After a verb it becomes voiced as 「がい」.

similar.title: 〜かいがある／〜かいもなく
similar.explanation: 「〜かいがある」 follows the ta-form or Noun + の (頑張ったかいがあった) and means “it wasn't for nothing”. 「〜がい」 follows the masu-stem and means the value of the act itself.

similar.title: 〜に値する
similar.explanation: 「〜に値する」 is an objective judgment of worth. 「〜がい」 is the doer's personal sense of reward.

similar.title: 〜甲斐性（かいしょう）
similar.explanation: 「甲斐性」 means “the ability to earn a living; being dependable”. It is a separate noun, unrelated to this pattern.

meaning: A spoken expression meaning something is so extreme it's hard to describe: “so ... you wouldn't believe it”, “incredibly ...”.
connection: Adjective / Verb plain form + のなんのって

senses.label: Incredibly ...
senses.meaning: The speaker stresses that a feeling is extremely strong. The rest is often left unsaid, or followed by a result like 「〜た」 or 「言葉にならない」. Vivid, exaggerated, and spoken.
senses.connection: い-adj / Verb plain form + のなんのって; な-adj + なのなんのって
examples: Yesterday's game was SO much fun.
My tooth hurt so badly that I couldn't sleep all night.
He suddenly showed up, and boy, was I surprised!

senses.label: Saying this and that
senses.meaning: 「〜のなんのと」 means “saying ... and so on”. Used to report someone's excuses or complaints, with annoyance.
senses.connection: Plain form + のなんのと(言って)
examples: He says he's busy or whatever, and won't help me.
All he does is complain that it's cold and so on.

notes: Very casual speech. Not used in formal situations or writing.
The sentence often ends right after 「のなんのって」, with intonation carrying the strong feeling.
With 「言う」, 「〜のなんのと」 means “making excuses, griping”, which is different from the degree use.

daily.title: Telling about a trip
daily.description: Exaggerating the cold to a friend.
daily.example: Hokkaido was so cold, I thought my nose would freeze.

daily.title: Recommending food
daily.description: Excitedly recommending a place.
daily.example: The ramen at that place is SO good!

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Saying your husband always makes excuses.
daily.example: My husband says he's tired or whatever and doesn't do any housework.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Talking about tough overtime.
work.example: Yesterday's overtime was so brutal, I almost collapsed.

etymology: Formed by listing 「〜の」 and 「なんの」 (“or what”) and adding the quoting 「って」. Originally “is it ... or what?”, it suggests the degree is too great to put into words, which gives emphasis.

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: 「〜といったらない」 also means an extreme degree, but is more formal and can be used in writing. 「〜のなんのって」 is very casual and exaggerated.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「〜てたまらない」 means your own feeling is unbearably strong; fine in ordinary conversation. 「〜のなんのって」 is more like exaggerated storytelling.

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: 「〜だの〜だの」 lists the complaints. 「〜のなんのと」 names only one and sums up the rest with 「なんの」. Both show annoyance.

title: 〜ようになっている (mechanism)
meaning: A machine, system, or thing is designed or set up to work this way: “is designed to ...”, “is set up so that ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようになっている

senses.label: How a device works
senses.meaning: Explains how a machine or device is built and works. Often with 「〜と」 or 「〜ば」: “when ..., it ...”.
senses.connection: 〜と／〜ば、Verb dictionary form + ようになっている
examples: This door is designed to open automatically when someone approaches.
If you press the button, hot water comes out.

senses.label: How a system is set up
senses.meaning: Explains how rules or systems are arranged: “it's set up so that ...”. Common in manuals and notices.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ようになっている
examples: Once you become a member, you can get discounts.
This room is set up so that only authorized people can enter.

senses.label: Natural mechanisms
senses.meaning: Explains functions the body or nature already has.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ようになっている
examples: The human body is made to sweat when it's hot.

notes: Different from 「〜ようになる」, which shows change (“now I can speak Japanese”). This describes a mechanism that is always there, not a change.
「〜ように作られている」 and 「〜ように設計されている」 are also used and make the human design clearer.
In speech, it often becomes 「〜ようになってる」.

daily.title: Teaching parents to use an appliance
daily.description: Explaining a rice cooker's feature.
daily.example: When the time comes, it cooks the rice automatically.

daily.title: At a hotel
daily.description: The front desk explaining the key card.
daily.example: When you insert the card, the lights turn on.

work.title: Explaining a product
work.description: Introducing a system to a client.
work.example: This system is designed to notify the administrator if there's a problem.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: Telling new employees about procedures.
work.example: Expenses are settled all at once at the end of the month.

etymology: Formed from 「ように」 (manner, state) + 「なっている」 (having become a state that continues). It means “is already in this state”, so it describes a thing's built-in structure or setup.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: 「〜ようになる」 shows a change in ability or habit (話せるようになった). 「〜ようになっている」 shows a mechanism or setup that is always there.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: 「〜ことになっている」 focuses on rules or agreements (it has been decided). 「〜ようになっている」 focuses on how something is built to work.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: 「〜ようにする」 is a person's conscious effort to make something happen. 「〜ようになっている」 describes an existing design or mechanism.

title: 〜という〜 (emphasizing amount)
meaning: Placed between a number word and a noun, it stresses how large a number or how long a time is: “as many as ...”, “a whole ...”.
connection: Number word + という + Noun (何百という人・数万という観客)

senses.label: Hundreds, thousands of ...
senses.meaning: With vague large numbers like 「何百」「何千」「数万」, it stresses that there are very many. It sounds amazed.
senses.connection: 何十・何百・何千・何万・数十・数万 + という + Noun
examples: Thousands of people gathered at the venue.
Tens of thousands of stars were shining in the sky.
I get hundreds of emails every day.

senses.label: Stressing an exact number
senses.meaning: With a specific number and counter, it stresses “that many / that long”. Common in the news and narration.
senses.connection: Number + counter + という + Noun (3万人という観客・10年という歳月)
examples: A full 50,000 spectators packed the stadium for the final.
It took a whole ten years to complete.

notes: Here 「という」 doesn't mean “called”; it emphasizes the amount.
The noun that follows is what the number counts (人・星・歳月).
「〜も」 (3時間も待った) also stresses a large amount, but 「という」 can only modify a noun.

daily.title: Talking about a concert
daily.description: Telling a friend how crowded it was.
daily.example: Tens of thousands of people came to the concert!

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A report on a large-scale event.
daily.example: Because of the typhoon, hundreds of flights were canceled.

work.title: Business report
work.description: Stressing the number of inquiries.
work.example: We've received thousands of inquiries about the new product.

work.title: Anniversary speech
work.description: Looking back on the company's history.
work.example: Fifty long years have passed since our founding.

etymology: 「という」 was originally a quoting expression meaning “called ...”. After a number word, it means roughly “amounting to ...”, which highlights the number and adds emphasis.

similar.title: 〜という (emphasizing all / amount)
similar.explanation: The N1 entry also covers repeating a noun for “every single ...”, as in 「家という家」 (every house). This entry covers only emphasis on amount.

similar.title: 〜という (called)
similar.explanation: 「山田という人」 means “a person called ...”, introducing a name. In this entry, a number comes first, to stress a large amount.

similar.title: 〜という〜 (every ...)
similar.explanation: 「町という町」 repeats the same noun to mean “every ...”. In this entry, it follows a number word.
